items.title: 2.5.3.1 Module Search Path and Package Structure

source_refs.note: Topic 2.5.3.1 Module Search Path and Package Structure (PDF 49-50, printed 46-47). Both steps are numbered '1.' in print; the function name prints as '1ist_products'.

blocks.text: When a module is imported, Python looks for it in order: first the current directory where the script is, then the standard library of built-in modules.

blocks.title: Python code (each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
# helper.py
def greet():
....return "As-Salaam-Alaikum from helper.py!"

# main.py (same folder)
import helper
print(helper.greet())

If the module is not in the current directory, Python looks in the standard library. random is part of the standard library, so it is found without any issue. The f before the string places the value of a variable inside the string.

blocks.title: Python code (each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
# main.py
import random
number = random.randint(1, 10)
print(f"Random number: {number}")    # any number from 1 to 10

blocks.title: Package
blocks.text: A package is a directory of related modules. For an e-commerce platform you could make a package ecommerce with modules products.py, customers.py and orders.py, and import with: from ecommerce import products.

blocks.title: Python code (each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
# ecommerce/products.py
def list_products():
....return ["Laptop", "Mobile", "Tablet"]

# main script
from ecommerce import products
available_products = products.list_products()
print(available_products)    # ['Laptop', 'Mobile', 'Tablet']
Organizing modules into packages is like arranging books into sections of a library: it makes code easier to find and maintain.
